title: Comparison of derivative-free optimization methods for groundwater supply and hydraulic capture community problems
contribution: Compares six derivative-free codes (APPS, Boeing Design Explorer, DIRECT-L, IFFCO, NOMAD with n+1/2n directions, NSGA-II) at default settings on two MODFLOW-based water-resources community problems (well-field supply, hydraulic capture), diagnoses failures, derives starting-point guidance and publishes a download page.
problem_entry: Application-community benchmark: the Mayer et al. community problems had not yet brought optimization experts' method classes into water resources or compared many methods on one problem; the field relies on GAs/simulated annealing (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: No new algorithm: the design goes into the comparison (heterogeneous portfolio described through one search-poll lens) and the formulation (inactive-well threshold, grid rounding, gradient-control constraints, linear-constraint violations returned as evaluation failures, stopping at the simulator's grid resolution) (pp. 9-16).
assumptions: Homogeneous unconfined aquifer, MODFLOW-96, 5-year horizon, cost model (9) with Table 1-2 data; author-chosen interpretations (200 m from Dirichlet boundaries, plume contour 5e-5 kg/m3, |Q|<1e-6 threshold) declared specific to this work; no convergence assumptions stated (pp. 5-10, 29).
proof_devices: no theorems; unproved feasibility claim that at least five wells are needed (p. 17)

landscape-mechanism argument: removing a well from a feasible six-well start requires a move that raises the objective beyond 'high frequency, low amplitude noise', motivating a starting-point rule (p. 21)
code-by-code status of barrier theory for linear vs nonlinear constraints (p. 14)
experiments: Best cost and evaluations to termination per code (Tables 3, 6), cost-vs-evaluations profiles (Figs. 2, 4), no run times, defaults only; 135 and 65 clustered feasible starts (DIRECT on feasibility, 50,000 evals, ~5,000 feasible points, AGNES) mostly fail; mechanism-based starts succeed; GA fails on 9 of 10 seeds; finite-difference interior-point code FDNIPS fails; no common budget (pp. 17-28).
positioning: Introduces deterministic 'sampling methods' with rigorous convergence to a GA/SA-dominated field, GA included for completeness; credits each code to its developers and concedes newer versions may be better (pp. 1, 4, 11).
writing: 15-author applied paper for a water audience; defines black-box formulation and surrogate-vs-approximation; places caveats next to results (1% spread vs 80% fixed cost); closes as 'a preliminary attempt' (pp. 9, 15, 19, 29).
limits_future: Global solutions unknown, no tuning, NOMAD stopped early on capture, fixed costs defeat surrogates/thresholds, interpretation specific; future: hybrid local-global methods, choosing the number of wells, handling fixed costs (pp. 3, 17, 26, 28-29).

title: OrthoMADS: a deterministic MADS instance with orthogonal directions
contribution: Introduces OrthoMADS, a MADS instance whose 2n poll directions are built deterministically (Halton vector, scale-and-round, scaled Householder) so they are integer, orthogonal and asymptotically dense, inheriting all MADS convergence results deterministically instead of with probability one; on 45 problems it scores at least as well as 30 LTMADS runs on most problems.
problem_entry: Two drawbacks of the authors' own LTMADS: random directions give convergence only with probability one, and Custodio-Vicente observed undesirably large angles / missed cones between poll directions (pp. 2, 22).
key_idea: Replace random poll construction by Halton u_t (from t=n+1) -> q = round(alpha(2u_t-e)/||2u_t-e||) with alpha by bisection so ||q|| <= 2^{|l|/2} -> H = ||q||^2 I - 2qq^T, D_k=[H -H]; index bookkeeping t_k = l_k+n+1 at the finest poll size so failed iterations run through the Halton tail; everything else identical to LTMADS (pp. 3-12).
assumptions: All MADS hypotheses inherited from [4]; extreme barrier for constraints; no new parameters; obligations reduce to the four MADS-instance properties (pp. 2, 14, 22).
proof_devices: framework-instance theorem: verify the four MADS-instance axioms and inherit all convergence results (Theorem 2.8, p. 14)
density chain: Halton dense (Prop. 2.1) + lower bound on alpha (Lemma 2.3) + rounding perturbation bound < eps/2 (Prop. 2.4) -> normalized q dense (Prop. 2.7) (pp. 5-14)
density transfer through Householder via explicit reflection vector d = (e_i - w)/sqrt(2(1-w_i)) with e_i - 2 d d_i = w (Prop. 2.6, pp. 9-10)
scaled Householder H = ||q||^2 I - 2qq^T gives an integer orthogonal basis (Prop. 2.5, pp. 8-9)
experiments: 45 problems (21 CUTEr smooth, 13 nonsmooth, 9 constrained, 2 real applications MDO/STY); LTMADS run 30 times, GPS/OrthoMADS scored by how many LTMADS runs they match or beat within 1%; 2n bases, opportunistic poll, optimist search only, stop at Delta^p < 1e-12 or 1000n evals; OrthoMADS average score 22.3 vs 13.5/14.2 for GPS; Rosenbrock direction-spread plots; final-value scoring, same-family competitors, no profiles (pp. 15-21).
positioning: Self-correction of LTMADS building on MADS [4] and its erratum [2]; reuses the critics' (Custodio-Vicente) test sets; Halton, Householder, Matousek cited as tools; no other DFO family cited (pp. 2, 14-15, 22-23).
writing: Abstract states the two advantages first; one running n=2 example threaded through all construction steps; tables of intermediate sequences; light hedging ('do seem', 'at least as competitive'); two-paragraph discussion without limitations (pp. 1-7, 22).
limits_future: No limitations or future work stated; reader: always 2n directions (minimal basis rejected), 'minimal' missed cones only illustrated, several inconsistencies between text, Figure 2 and Table 3 (pp. 10-12, 21-22).

title: A progressive barrier for derivative-free nonlinear programming
contribution: Proposes MADS-PB: squared constraint violations aggregated into h, a non-increasing barrier h^max_k, feasible and infeasible incumbents with filter-style dominance, and polling around both; proves a hierarchy of Clarke-type results for f and h, gives a counterexample motivating a new constraint qualification, and shows faster progress than two-phase MADS-EB from infeasible starts.
problem_entry: Own GPS-filter has weak theory and MADS-EB needs feasible starts; four user situations (no feasible start in aircraft planform, sensitivity information, failing/Boolean industrial codes, disjoint domains) justify keeping infeasible points (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Progressively tighten a threshold on aggregated violation, keeping best feasible and best undominated infeasible incumbents; iterations classified dominating/improving/unsuccessful; h^max_0 = 0 with a feasible start recovers MADS-EB; closed (always) vs open (at solution) constraints (pp. 2-13).
assumptions: A1 initial point in X with finite f and h < h^max_0; A2 bounded trial points; A3 external CQ (h°(x;v) < 0 near x-hat for hypertangent v) introduced after a counterexample, sufficient not necessary; local Lipschitz, nonempty hypertangent cone, dense refining directions (LTMADS, with probability 1) (pp. 5, 12, 14, 21, 24).
proof_devices: three-case analysis: feasible refining subsequence, infeasible subsequence (results on h), infeasible converging to feasible (pp. 15-23)
standard MADS Clarke-derivative argument with t_k = Delta^m_k||d_k|| and y_k = x_k + t_k(d_k/||d_k|| - v) plus limsup split (Thm 3.3, pp. 16-17)
mirror proof swapping (f, Omega) for (h, X) (Thm 3.5, p. 18)
adversarial but legal Search step producing a bad limit on a 1-D C^1 constraint built from a rescaled quintic (Example 3.7, Prop. 3.8 by induction, pp. 19-21)
A3 related to smooth CQs via h° = 2 v^T C'(x)^T W(x) C(x) (Thm 3.10, pp. 21-22)
unsuccessful iteration + decreasing h forces feasible poll points -> infinitely many feasible points (Thm 3.12, p. 23)
experiments: GPS-EB, GPS-filter, LTMADS-EB, LTMADS-PB with 1 or 2 secondary directions; 5 seeds averaged; feasible and infeasible starts; two-phase EB evaluations counted; 600n budget; convex hypersphere and nonconvex problems n=5..50, h^max_0 sweep giving a default rule, Table 1 first-feasible vs best (n=50: EB 1004 evals f=-22.2, PB 2401.9 evals f=-46.0), STYRENE (8 vars, 4 closed, 7 open, may fail); no spread, no profiles (pp. 25-32).
positioning: Continues Fletcher-Leyffer filter via own GPS-filter and MADS-EB; uses dominance but no filter; relates CQ to Gould-Tolle/MFCQ and SQP assumptions; calls earlier GPS approaches noncompetitive; credits Paul Frank (Boeing) for the frame-center trigger (pp. 2-3, 14, 21, 33).
writing: Abstract positions by 'As in... As in... unlike...'; four-bullet motivation answering 'why not keep the barrier'; plain-words promise before definitions; (h,f)-plane figures; theory summarized as a ladder; discussion more cautious than abstract ('We need more tests') (pp. 1-4, 14, 24, 32-33).
limits_future: Not better from feasible starts, wasted infeasible evaluations in one case, more tests needed, A3 not necessary, proofs (v)-(x) omitted; only future hint: surrogates (pp. 24-25, 32-33).

quotes.text: An extreme barrier algorithm rejects all infeasible trial points. A progressive barrier algorithm places a threshold on the constraint violation it allows, and progressively tightens this threshold as the algorithm progresses.
We need more tests, but we tentatively conclude that since LTMADS-PB is better from infeasible starts and about the same from feasible starts, it is the better choice.

title: Blackbox and derivative-free optimization: theory, algorithms and applications
contribution: Two-page special-issue editorial that defines blackbox vs derivative-free optimization, positions DFO as a fallback to gradient methods and as more rigorous than heuristics, orders the issue from applications to theory, and lists anticipated research topics.
problem_entry: Definitional and timing-based: growing interest over the last decade justifies a special issue; blackbox = structure cannot be exploited, DFO = only function values (p. 1).
key_idea: DFO algorithms are not competitors of gradient methods but a fallback; rigorous DFO with convergence properties beats heuristics whose solutions cannot be characterized (pp. 1-2).
assumptions: No formal model; scope is expensive simulation-based design where reliable gradients are unavailable (p. 1).
positioning: Two foils: gradient-based methods (to be used when gradients are available) and heuristics (popular but uncharacterizable); historical anchors Fermi-Metropolis 1952 and Nelder-Mead 1965 (pp. 1-2).
writing: Short declarative sentences, one 'It is obvious that' concession, hedged 'crystal ball' forecast, persuasion aimed at engineers ('modest investment') (pp. 1-2).
limits_future: No limits stated; anticipated topics: stochastic/noisy problems, parallelism for large problems, multifidelity models and surrogates, explicit analytical equality/inequality constraints, hybrid strategies for escaping local solutions (p. 2).

quotes.text: Blackbox and derivative-free algorithms are not competitors of gradient-based methods; they are a fallback when gradient-based algorithms cannot be used.
The latter are popular because they are easy to understand and implement, but their solutions can rarely be characterized in terms of optimality or quality.
